text.p: French electrical appliance company Moulinex confirmed on Monday that it planned to cut jobs by 22 percent but said it would try to avoid layoffs by introducing flexible schedules and reorganising manufacturing activities.

After a stormy meeting on Friday with staff representatives, Moulinex confirmed the broad outlines of a restructuring plan announced in June entailing 2,600 job cuts -- 2,100 in France -- and the closure of two French plants.
The company, led by new chairman Pierre Blayau, said the drastic restructuring was crucial to cutting costs and attaining productivity levels similar to those of its competitors.

Blayau said the restructuring would be accompanied by an aggressive marketing campaign. "We're planning to introduce five important products in the near future," he said in an interview with the newspaper Liberation on Monday.
Moulinex seeks to avoid outright sackings through employee transfers, a 15 percent reduction in work hours and flexible schedules, early retirement and relocation assistance programmes.
"These four measures are indispensable to attain the zero layoff objective," the company said in a statement.
In exchange for the reduction in work hours, the government would reduce charges on the company by eight percent over three years.
The employee transfers would occur as part of a reorganisation of activities at Moulinex's manufacturing plants aimed at lowering costs by increasing specialisation.

Under the new plan, microwave ovens would be made at the Cormelles plant, chip fryers in Bayeux, coffee makers and irons at Alencon, vacuum cleaners at Falaise, blenders in Mayenne, steamers in Fresnay and electric motors at Saint Lo.

The company confirmed plans to close the Argentan plant, which makes microwaves and deep fryers, and the Mamers factory, which produces blenders, plastic parts, irons, mixers, coffee makers and motors.

Moulinex would expand activities at its Mexican plant which sells mostly to the U.S. market, concentrate toaster production at its Spanish facility, small blenders at its Irish plant and coffee makers at its German facilities.

The company reiterated its goals to generate operating profit of between eight and nine percent of turnover, up from 0.5 percent, and increase sales to nine billion francs within three years, up from 7.8 billion for the year ended on March 31.
In June the company reported a loss for 1995/96 of 702 million francs, its fourth consecutive annual loss, after taking a 600 million charge for the restructuring plan.
